Artist/Creator (supplementary): The Palais Lascaris is a seventeenth-century aristocratic building in Nice, France. Currently, it is a musical instrument museum. Located in the old town of Nice, it houses a collection of over 500 instruments, which makes it France’s second most important collection after the Musée de la Musique de la Philharmonie in Paris.


== History ==

Orientation: Stand directly in front of the Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore, dated 1717, within the Palais Lascaris. From this vantage point, you can appreciate the instrument's elegant contours and the masterful craftsmanship that defines it.

In 1901, Antoine Gautier, a passionate collector and amateur musician, bequeathed his collection of musical instruments, including this exquisite bass viol, to the city of Nice. Officially welcomed into the municipal collections in 1904, the instruments found their permanent residence at the Palais Lascaris in 1970, when the Gautier collection was transferred here. This move enriched the museum's offerings, cementing its status as the home of France's second most important collection of musical instruments.

This bass viol, crafted by Paolo Antonio Testore, is a testament to the Italian luthier's skill. Larger than a modern cello, it embodies the precision and artistry of Milanese instrument-making. Testore's work at the sign of the Eagle in Milan during the early 18th century set a benchmark in string instrument craftsmanship. This petite basse de violon, with its intricate scroll and varnished finish, showcases the transition from the viola da gamba family to the modern violin family. Just as the violes gambe by William Turner you previously encountered echo the English tradition, this instrument reflects the Italian mastery that influenced future orchestral developments. At Palais Lascaris, this bass viol stands as a testament to the enduring legacy of musical innovation and craftsmanship.

Orientation: As you stand before William Turner's striking six-string bass viola da gamba, let your eyes linger on the intricate carvings of its head and pegbox. This vantage point will reveal the artistry that has kept it a treasured part of musical history.

Crafted in 1652 by the English luthier William Turner at his workshop in Gravel Lane near Aldgate, this viola da gamba has a story distinct from many of its contemporaries. Unlike other 17th-century viols that were later modified into cellos, this instrument remains largely unaltered, preserving its original carved head and pegbox. Its survival in this state is a testament to its craftsmanship and historical significance. This viol became a part of Nice's public collections thanks to the bequest of Antoine Gautier, a devoted collector who passed away in 1904. Today, it resides in the Palais Lascaris, where it is maintained in playable condition and occasionally used for live concert performances.

The viol's presence here adds a unique dimension to the Palais Lascaris's collection of over 500 instruments. Its continued playability connects us to the soundscape of 17th-century England, offering a resonant echo of the past. The viol's intricate woodwork and six-string configuration exemplify the technical prowess of its maker, while its enduring condition highlights the significance of preservation in musical heritage.

Reflecting on the viols you've already encountered, like the sackbut from Nuremberg, the viola da gamba showcases the evolutionary journey of string instruments. It stands as a reminder of the rich, resonant tones that captured the imagination of English composers and audiences alike in the 17th century. As you ponder this, consider what innovations in string instruments might have emerged from Italy's renowned craftsmanship, continuing the story of musical evolution.

This exquisite instrument eventually came into the possession of the Viscountess of Beaumont, a French aristocrat of the 18th century. Over time, it was forgotten and ended up stored in the attic of the Château de Busset in the Allier department of France. In 1995, the harp was rediscovered there, bringing it back into the world of music and history. Subsequently, in 2007, the City of Nice purchased the harp, and it now resides in the permanent collection of the Musée du Palais Lascaris, where it continues to captivate visitors with its beauty and history.

Orientation: Stand before the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) at the Palais Lascaris in Nice, France, and let your eyes trace the elegant curves of this 18th-century masterpiece. From this vantage point, the intricate carvings and gilded embellishments reveal themselves in their full splendor, offering a glimpse into the opulence of the French court on the eve of the Revolution.

In 1780, Jean-Henri Naderman, a celebrated luthier from Westphalia, crafted this harp in Paris. It found its place in the hands of the Viscountess of Beaumont, a prominent figure in the French aristocracy of the time. As years passed, the harp was forgotten and stored away in the attic of the Château de Busset in the Allier department of France. In a stroke of serendipity, it was rediscovered in 1995, bringing back its historical and musical significance. The City of Nice acquired the harp in 2007, and it now graces the permanent collection of the Musée du Palais Lascaris.

The harp stands as a testament to the craftsmanship of its era, constructed from carved, painted, and gilded wood. Its soundboard is adorned with symmetrical floral motifs, and a landscape scene is framed by sculpted acanthus leaves at the base. This single-action pedal harp operates using a traditional crochet mechanism, allowing the musician to shorten strings by a semitone, a technique that was revolutionary during its time.

The Palais Lascaris itself, a baroque gem in the old town of Nice, houses over 500 historical instruments, making it the second most important collection of musical instruments in France after the Musée de la Musique de la Philharmonie in Paris. This setting enhances the harp's legacy, connecting it to a broader narrative of musical innovation and aristocratic culture. As you stand before this instrument, consider what melodies might have echoed through the halls of French salons before the Revolution, offering a poignant reminder of a bygone era.

Orientation: Stand before the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer from 1581, an artifact that captures the transition from medieval to Renaissance music. From this vantage point, you will see the intricate craftsmanship that has endured through the centuries.

The tenor sackbut, crafted by Anton Schnitzer in 1581, was initially part of a private collection. In 1901, it became part of the public collections of Nice through the bequest of Antoine Gautier, a local amateur musician and collector. This donation ensured the instrument's preservation in its original state, and it eventually found a permanent home in the Palais Lascaris in 2001, where it remains a rare example of a 16th-century trombone with its original mouthpiece intact.

This exquisite instrument, an ancestor of the modern trombone, is a testament to the skill and artistry of its maker, Anton Schnitzer the Elder, a renowned brass instrument craftsman active in Nuremberg during the late 16th century. The sackbut's slender brass body, with an acoustically effective bore diameter of 10 mm, showcases Schnitzer's meticulous attention to detail. The bell rim bears his mark and inscription, 'MACHT ANTONI SCHNITZER A[NNO] MDLXXXI,' serving as a signature of authenticity and craftsmanship.

The historical significance of this sackbut extends beyond its craftsmanship. It represents a pivotal moment in the evolution of brass instruments, bridging the gap between medieval and Renaissance music. Unlike many instruments of its time that underwent heavy modifications, this sackbut has survived in its acoustically original state, making it the oldest surviving sackbut in the world. Its presence here at the Palais Lascaris connects it to a broader narrative of musical evolution, similar to the harp by Naderman from Paris, 1780, which you have already seen.

As you ponder the evolution of music and instruments, consider how the artistry of string instruments, like the harp, developed alongside these brass giants. Each piece in this collection tells a story of innovation and tradition, inviting us to explore the rich tapestry of music's history.

Orientation: Position yourself just to the right of the instrument to appreciate the curvature of the back and the intricate craftsmanship of the neck, which reveals Paolo Antonio Testore's mastery of the luthier's art.

In 1901, collector and amateur musician Antoine Gautier bequeathed his collection of musical instruments, including the Testore basse de violon, to the city of Nice. This generous act was officially accepted by the city in September 1904, ensuring the instruments became part of the municipal collections of Nice. In 1970, the Gautier collection was transferred to the newly opened museum at the Palais Lascaris, enriching the museum's offerings and providing a permanent home for these historical instruments. This bass viol, crafted by Paolo Antonio Testore in Milan in 1717, exemplifies the Italian mastery of string instruments. Testore, following in the footsteps of his father, Carlo Giuseppe, honed his craft in Milan, contributing to the family's esteemed reputation in instrument-making. Unlike the violas da gamba you saw earlier, this instrument is larger than a modern cello and embodies the precision and artistry of Milanese instrument-making. Its presence here, among France's second most important collection of musical instruments, connects the dots between the evolution of string instruments and their pivotal role in orchestral developments.

Orientation: As you stand here, notice the delicate craftsmanship of the viola da gamba by William Turner, an instrument whose rich history resonates throughout this room.

In 1652, the English luthier William Turner crafted a six-string bass viola da gamba in his London workshop located in Gravel Lane near Aldgate. Unlike many other viols from the 17th century that were later altered into cellos, this particular bass viol remained largely in its original condition, preserving its original carved head and pegbox. Antoine Gautier, a Niçois amateur musician and collector, bequeathed this viol to the city of Nice in 1904, ensuring its preservation and public display. Gautier, born in 1825, played the violin and viola, and founded a musical quartet with his brother Raymond at age eighteen. Turner's viol, part of this generous bequest, is now displayed at the Palais Lascaris. It continues to be maintained in playable condition and has been used for live concert performances in the palace's salons, offering audiences a rare auditory glimpse into the musical past. As you recall the sackbut you stopped at a moment ago, consider the evolution of string instruments — a journey that continues into the next room with stunning examples of Italian craftsmanship.

Orientation: Stand close to the harp's intricate soundboard, where you can truly appreciate the craftsmanship of Jean-Henri Naderman. Observe the carved and gilded wood, the floral motifs, and the landscape scene framed by sculpted acanthus leaves, elements that embody the refined elegance of 18th-century Paris.

In 1780, Jean-Henri Naderman, a celebrated luthier from Westphalia, crafted this harp in Paris, bringing his expertise and artistry to a city renowned for its musical innovations. The harp then found its way into the hands of the Viscountess of Beaumont, a prominent figure in the French aristocracy, symbolizing the opulence of the pre-Revolutionary era. Over time, the harp was forgotten and stored away in the attic of the Château de Busset in the Allier department of France. In a delightful twist of fate, it was rediscovered in 1995, restoring its historical and musical significance.

The City of Nice purchased this exquisite instrument in 2007, bringing it into the permanent collection of the Musée du Palais Lascaris. Here, it stands as a testament to an era of both artistic refinement and dramatic change, captivating visitors with its beauty and history. Constructed of carved, painted, and gilded wood, the harp operates on a single-action pedal mechanism. This traditional crochet mechanism allows for semitone adjustments, showcasing the technical prowess of Naderman's craftsmanship.

Among the vast array of instruments in the Palais Lascaris, this harp connects to the broader narrative of musical history. Housing the second most important collection of musical instruments in France, after the Musée de la Musique de la Philharmonie in Paris, the Palais Lascaris offers a unique glimpse into the past. This harp, with its delicate strings and elegant design, echoes an era right before the French Revolution, a time when music was both a personal joy and a societal statement.

What other instruments, one wonders, filled these halls with music before the harp's delicate strings came to life again?

Orientation: Stand directly in front of the Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore, crafted in Milan in 1717. From this vantage point, the intricate curves and the aged patina of the wood reveal the expertise embedded in its creation, a tribute to the Testore family's legacy.

In 1901, Antoine Gautier, a passionate collector and amateur musician, bequeathed his impressive collection, including the Testore basse de violon, to the city of Nice. This gift, officially accepted by the city in September 1904, secured the instruments as part of Nice’s municipal collections. Paolo Antonio Testore, building upon his father Carlo Giuseppe's teachings in Milan, honed his luthier skills to create this bass viol, a larger predecessor to the modern cello. Gautier’s collection found a new home in 1970 at the newly opened museum at the Palais Lascaris, which houses France's second-most important collection of musical instruments.

Testore’s craftsmanship is evident in the instrument’s elegant form and rich tone, a testament to the Milanese tradition of string instrument making. The bass viol complements the variety of string instruments you’ve seen, including the Turner viol from London. As you view it, consider its historical context and the evolving demands of orchestral life. Testore's work not only shows the artistry of the period but also encapsulates the transition to modern orchestral sounds.

Orientation: As you approach the viola da gamba by William Turner, notice its rich wood grain and finely carved head, features that are best appreciated from a close vantage point.

In 1652, the English luthier William Turner crafted this six-string bass viola da gamba in his London workshop on Gravel Lane near Aldgate. Unlike many other 17th-century viols later converted into cellos, this instrument remains largely intact, retaining its original carved head and pegbox. Antoine Gautier, an enthusiastic amateur musician from Nice, acquired this rare piece and later bequeathed it to the city in 1904, significantly enriching the local collection. Today, the viol is a centerpiece at the Palais Lascaris, maintained in playable condition and featured in live performances. It stands as a testament to the enduring legacy and craftsmanship of 17th-century England. The viol reflects a time when such instruments captured the imagination of English composers and audiences, much like the sacqueboute tenor you admired earlier. 

The viol's presence in the Palais Lascaris not only complements the museum's extensive collection of over 500 instruments but also invites us to appreciate the interconnected history of European musical craftsmanship.

Orientation: Stand before the glass case housing the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, made in Nuremberg in 1581. From this vantage point, observe the instrument's original brass mouthpiece and the maker's inscription on its bell rim.

The tenor sackbut, crafted by Anton Schnitzer in 1581, was initially part of a private collection. This remarkable instrument became part of the public collections of Nice through the bequest of Antoine Gautier in 1901, a local amateur musician and collector. Gautier's donation ensured the instrument's preservation in its original state, and it eventually found a permanent home in the Palais Lascaris in 2001, where it remains a rare example of a 16th-century trombone with its original mouthpiece intact.

Anton Schnitzer specialized in creating ceremonial brass instruments for the Bavarian court, with this sackbut standing as a testament to his expertise. The bell rim bears the inscription 'MACHT ANTONI SCHNITZER A[NNO] MDLXXXI,' marking its provenance and the meticulous craftsmanship that went into its creation. The tenor sackbut's slender brass body, with an acoustically effective bore diameter of 10 mm, showcases Schnitzer's meticulous attention to sound production, which continues to resonate through history.

This instrument bridges the medieval and Renaissance musical traditions, predating modern trombones. The Palais Lascaris, a seventeenth-century aristocratic building, now serves as a bastion for musical history, housing over 500 instruments. As you continue to explore, consider how such brass instruments evolved alongside the stringed harp you encountered earlier, charting the dynamic interplay between musical forms through the centuries.

Orientation: For a moment, stand back and let your eyes trace the elegant lines of the Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore (Milan, 1717). From this vantage point, its graceful proportions and refined craftsmanship emerge with clarity, a testament to the finesse of Milanese luthiers.

In 1901, the collector and amateur musician Antoine Gautier bequeathed his collection of musical instruments, including the Testore basse de violon, to the city of Nice. This generous act was officially accepted by the city in September 1904, ensuring the instruments became part of the municipal collections of Nice. Carlo Giuseppe Testore, Paolo Antonio’s father, established a renowned workshop in Milan after studying under Giovanni Grancino. This foundation allowed Paolo Antonio to produce exquisite instruments like this bass viol, blending his father's teachings with his own innovations. In 1970, the Gautier collection was transferred to the newly opened museum at the Palais Lascaris, preserving its legacy and enhancing the museum's status as a home for France’s second most important collection of musical instruments.

The instrument itself is a petite basse de violon, a precursor to the modern cello, yet larger and more resonant. Its presence in this collection not only showcases the artistry of the Testore family but also serves as a bridge to the violes de gambe by William Turner you admired earlier. Each piece in this vibrant collection adds another layer to the rich tapestry of musical history housed within these walls.

Orientation: As you stand before the viola da gamba by William Turner, notice the intricate carving on the original pegbox—it’s an exquisite detail often overlooked, yet it whispers stories of its 17th-century origins.

In 1652, William Turner, an English luthier, crafted this six-string bass viola da gamba in his workshop in Gravel Lane, London, showcasing the meticulous craftsmanship of the period. Unlike many viols of its era, this instrument remained unmodified, preserving its original carved head and pegbox. This untouched state became key when it entered the public collection of Nice through a generous bequest by Antoine Gautier, a Niçois amateur musician and collector, in 1904. Gautier, who assembled an impressive collection of over 500 instruments, including the sackbut you stopped at earlier, chose to enrich his city's cultural heritage with these donations. Today, the viol is not just a display piece at the Palais Lascaris; it’s maintained in playable condition and even used in live performances, resonating its rich, haunting tones in the palace's historic salons. Turner's viol stands as a living artifact, a testament to England's vibrant 17th-century musical scene and the foresight of collectors like Gautier, who shaped cultural legacies that endure to this day.

Orientation: Stand back and take in the full length of the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) at the Palais Lascaris. This vantage point reveals the intricate landscape scene framed by sculpted acanthus leaves at the base, an ornate touch that speaks to the opulence of pre-Revolutionary France.

In the bustling city of Paris in 1780, Jean-Henri Naderman, a luthier originally from Westphalia, crafted this harp. His creation soon found a prestigious owner in the Viscountess of Beaumont, a member of the French aristocracy, confirming the instrument's place within elite circles. As time passed, however, the harp became a forgotten relic, stored away in the attic of the Château de Busset in the Allier department of France. It was in 1995 that a twist of fate brought the harp back into the light, rediscovering it for both the historical and music-loving communities.

Constructed from carved, painted, and gilded wood, this harp exemplifies the artistic finesse of its era, with a soundboard adorned in symmetrical floral motifs. The single-action pedal mechanism, utilizing the traditional crochet system, showcases the technology of the time, allowing the harpist to raise the pitch of strings by a semitone. In 2007, the City of Nice recognized the value of this historical piece and purchased it, ensuring its preservation as part of the permanent collection at the Musée du Palais Lascaris.

The Palais Lascaris itself is a jewel of historical and cultural significance, housing the second most important collection of musical instruments in France, only surpassed by the Musée de la Musique in Paris. This harp stands among over 500 instruments in the museum, from the 18th century to the modern day, highlighting the evolution of musical craftsmanship. As you absorb the elegance of Naderman's work, ponder the melodies it must have played, echoing through the grand salons of its time.

Orientation: Stand close to the Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore, displayed in the Palais Lascaris. From this perspective, you'll appreciate the intricate craftsmanship that reveals the work's role in the evolution of string instruments.

In 1901, the collector and amateur musician Antoine Gautier bequeathed his collection of musical instruments, including the Testore basse de violon, to the city of Nice. This generous donation was officially accepted by the city in September 1904, securing the instruments as part of the municipal collections. By 1970, the Gautier collection had found a new permanent home at the newly opened museum at the Palais Lascaris, enhancing the institution's role as France's second most important collection of musical instruments.

The bass viol in front of you is a creation of Paolo Antonio Testore, crafted in Milan around 1717. Testore, inheriting the trade from his father Carlo Giuseppe Testore—an esteemed luthier known for his precision—produced this instrument, which illustrates the bridge between tradition and innovation in music. The petite basse de violon was larger than a modern cello, yet served as an essential precursor to later orchestral developments. Orientation: As you approach William Turner's viola da gamba, crafted in London in 1652, notice how the light catches its original carved head and pegbox, reflecting its nearly untouched state over the centuries.

In 1652, the English luthier William Turner crafted a six-string bass viola da gamba in his workshop located in Gravel Lane near Aldgate. Unlike many other viols from the 17th century that were later modified into cellos, this particular bass viol remained largely in its original condition, preserving its original carved head and pegbox. Antoine Gautier, a dedicated Niçois amateur musician and avid collector, bequeathed the viol to the public collections of Nice in 1904, allowing it to become a cherished part of the Palais Lascaris. The instrument is not merely a static display piece; it is maintained in playable condition and has been used for live concert performances in the palace's salons, keeping its rich sound alive for modern audiences. This addition enriches the museum's impressive collection of over 500 instruments, offering an audible link to the musical past. Now imagine what innovation came next — the viols and violins crafted by Italian artisans known for their unparalleled craftsmanship.

Orientation: Stand close to the tenor sackbut by Anton Schnitzer (Nuremberg, 1581), allowing you to see the maker's inscription on the bell rim and appreciate the untouched elegance that has persisted through centuries.

The tenor sackbut crafted by Anton Schnitzer in 1581 holds a fascinating tale of preservation and legacy. Originally part of a private collection, this remarkably intact instrument entered the public collections of Nice in 1901, thanks to the bequest of Antoine Gautier, a local amateur musician and collector. Gautier's donation ensured not only the sackbut's preservation but also enriched Nice's cultural heritage. In 2001, it found its permanent place at the Palais Lascaris, a museum renowned for its dedication to historical musical instruments.

Schnitzer, a master craftsman active in Nuremberg between 1557 and 1608, produced this extraordinary piece with precision, its slender brass body and original mouthpiece making it one of the rarest surviving 16th-century trombones. The instrument's bore diameter of 10 mm speaks to the meticulous care prevalent in that era's instrument-making, echoing the skill seen in Schnitzer's other works, which served the Bavarian court's ceremonial needs.

The bell rim bears Schnitzer's hallmark, inscribed 'MACHT ANTONI SCHNITZER A[NNO] MDLXXXI,' signalling its provenance and the artistry that has survived the sands of time. This piece stands as a bridge between the medieval sackbut and the modern trombone, paralleling the harp from your earlier stop, which reflects the evolution of string instruments. As you consider the position of the sackbut within this vast collection, it prompts a reflection on how string and brass instruments have evolved alongside one another.

Orientation: Stand before "Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780)" within the grandeur of Palais Lascaris, and let your eyes trace the elegant curves and intricate details that tell a story of craftsmanship and historical journey.

In 1780, Jean-Henri Naderman crafted this harp in Paris, channeling his mastery as a luthier originally from the Westphalia region. This creation became the prized possession of the Viscountess of Beaumont, a prominent French aristocrat whose interest in music mirrored the opulent tastes of her era. Over time, the harp was forgotten, relegated to an attic in the Château de Busset in the Allier department of France. The intricate woodwork, carved and gilded, encapsulates the Parisian elegance of its time, featuring a soundboard adorned with floral motifs and a landscape scene framed by sculpted acanthus leaves.

In 1995, the harp was rescued from obscurity, rediscovered in that very attic, rekindling its historical significance and musical charm. The City of Nice strategically purchased this remarkable instrument in 2007, ensuring its preservation in the Musée du Palais Lascaris. This acquisition placed the harp in the second most important collection of musical instruments in France, after the Muséee de la Musique de la Philharmonie in Paris, alongside over 500 others in the Palais's permanent collection. This collection transformed Palais Lascaris from a 17th-century aristocratic residence into a vibrant music museum, showcasing a rich tapestry of musical history.

Jean-Henri Naderman's harp, with its single-action pedal mechanism, allows players to raise the pitch by a semitone using a traditional crochet system. This design innovation was a precursor to the more complex double-action mechanisms that would later revolutionize harp music by enabling greater versatility in composition and performance. As you contemplate the harp's ornate beauty, consider how Naderman's creation could evoke the grandeur of pre-Revolution France. Yet, alongside this harp, Palais Lascaris whispers of melodies played by other instruments in its echoes, resonating across centuries of musical heritage.

Orientation: Stand close to the display enclosing the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, allowing you to observe the intricate markings on its bell rim. From this vantage, the nuances of Schnitzer's craftsmanship—the slender brass body and the original mouthpiece—are most apparent.

The tenor sackbut crafted by Anton Schnitzer in 1581 was initially part of a private collection. In 1901, it became part of the public collections of Nice through the bequest of Antoine Gautier, a local amateur musician and collector. This donation ensured the instrument's preservation in its original state, and it eventually found a permanent home in the Palais Lascaris in 2001, where it remains a rare example of a 16th-century trombone with its original mouthpiece intact. 

Schnitzer, known for his expertise in brass instrument-making, crafted this sackbut in Nuremberg, a city renowned for its musical instruments in the 16th century. The sackbut's slender brass body, with an acoustically effective bore diameter of 10 mm, showcases Schnitzer’s meticulous attention to acoustical precision. Unlike many surviving instruments from the 16th century, this sackbut exists in its original condition, untouched by the modifications that often befell brass instruments over time. 

The bell rim bears the maker’s inscription, ‘MACHT ANTONI SCHNITZER A[NNO] MDLXXXI’, and his workshop device mark, affirming its authenticity and origin. Before its placement in Palais Lascaris, the instrument was part of the Conservatoire National de Région de Nice. The sackbut shares its historical significance with the harp from 1780 you encountered earlier, marking the evolution of music from the Renaissance through to the Classical era. As you ponder the technical and artistic feats achieved by craftsmen like Schnitzer, consider how different musical eras influenced each other, sculpting the sounds that have resonated throughout centuries. This leads us to contemplate how string instruments, like the harp, developed alongside their brass counterparts.

Orientation: Stand by the intricately carved and gilded woodwork of the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) at Palais Lascaris to appreciate the delicate floral motifs and the sculpted acanthus leaves on its base. From this vantage point, the detail and craftsmanship of Jean-Henri Naderman are fully visible, bringing to life the elegance of 18th-century Parisian design.

In 1780, Jean-Henri Naderman, a master luthier from Westphalia, produced this harp in his Parisian workshop, showcasing his extraordinary skill in musical instrument craftsmanship. The harp became part of French high society when it was owned by the Viscountess of Beaumont, embedding itself into the opulence of the period. However, over the years, it was neglected and relegated to an attic in the Château de Busset, nestled in the Allier department of France. It remained there, hidden from the world, until 1995, when it was rediscovered, reigniting interest in its historical and cultural significance. By 2007, the City of Nice had acquired the harp, adding it to the prestigious collection at the Musée du Palais Lascaris, a repository for musical treasures and France's second most important collection of historical instruments, following the Musée de la Musique de la Philharmonie in Paris.

The harp is a single-action pedal instrument, utilizing the traditional crochet mechanism to alter the pitch—a testament to the technical innovations of its time. The soundboard, adorned with harmonious floral patterns and a pastoral landscape scene, underscores the artistic and decorative aesthetics of late 18th-century France. Here, amidst the Palais Lascaris' extensive collection of over 500 instruments, Naderman's harp stands not only as a work of art but also as a symbol of the musical grandeur that preluded the French Revolution. The restoration efforts further enhanced its magnificence, allowing its visual and acoustic beauty to shine. This harp, with its rich narrative of creation, ownership, neglect, and rediscovery, echoes the sounds of an era while continuing to captivate and inspire.

There, the long-forgotten harp crafted by Jean-Henri Naderman in 1780 was found, having been out of sight for many years. This rediscovery led to the harp's eventual acquisition by the City of Nice in 2007, allowing it to be preserved and displayed in the Musée du Palais Lascaris. As a result, this exquisite instrument now stands as a testament to Naderman's craftsmanship, accessible to the public for appreciation and study.

Orientation: Position yourself close to the glass case where the Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore (Milan, 1696) is displayed. From this vantage point, the intricate woodwork and craftsmanship of the instrument reveal the meticulous artistry that Testore brought to each creation.

In 1901, Antoine Gautier, a collector and amateur musician, bequeathed his collection of musical instruments, including the Testore basse de violon, to the city of Nice. This collection was officially accepted by the city in September 1904. Then, in 1970, the City of Nice transferred the Gautier collection to the newly opened museum at the Palais Lascaris. Because of this transfer, the instrument now resides in a historical monument, enriching the cultural tapestry of Nice.

The instrument itself, classified as a petite basse de violon, is an early bass member of the violin family, larger than a modern cello. Crafted in Milan, it embodies the Italian mastery of string instruments, as seen in the rich grain of the wood and the elegant curvature of its body. This bass viol stands as a testament to Paolo Antonio Testore's lineage, rooted in the teachings of his father, Carlo Giuseppe Testore, who founded their workshop in Milan. The Testore family was known for producing instruments that were both beautiful and functional, and this piece is no exception. Its continued presence here at Palais Lascaris not only underscores the museum's role as a guardian of musical heritage but also connects back to the violes gambe by William Turner that you admired earlier, illustrating the evolution of string instruments from the 17th century to the present.

Orientation: As you stand before the viola da gamba by William Turner, place yourself to the side to appreciate the intricate carving on its pegbox. This angle offers a view of the original headpiece, a rare survival from the 17th century, and highlights the instrument's rich patina, a testament to its centuries-long journey.

This six-string bass viola da gamba was crafted in 1652 by the English luthier William Turner. Unlike many viols of its time, which were later transformed into cellos to suit evolving musical tastes, this instrument has retained its original form. Its survival in such pristine condition is thanks to a bequest from Antoine Gautier, a Niçois musician, in 1904. Now housed in the Palais Lascaris, it is not just a static exhibit but is maintained in playable condition. This ensures it continues to vibrate through time, echoing the music of the past during live concerts in the palace's salons, connecting listeners to its rich auditory history.

The presence of the viola da gamba in Nice is more than just an addition to the museum's collection of over 500 instruments. It represents the intersection of English craftsmanship and European musical heritage. Unlike the sackbut you saw earlier, which showcased the brass innovations of Nuremberg, this viol speaks to England's 17th-century musical culture, where its resonant tones captured the imagination of composers and audiences alike. As you contemplate this instrument, consider the innovations in string instruments that Italian craftsmanship later brought to the forefront.

Orientation: Stand before the Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore, focusing on its intricate craftsmanship. From this vantage point, the elegance of its curves and the rich patina of its wood reveal themselves, echoing the legacy of Italian luthiers.

In 1901, Antoine Gautier, a collector and amateur musician, bequeathed his collection of musical instruments, including the Testore basse de violon, to the city of Nice. This collection was officially accepted by the city in September 1904. Then, in 1970, the City of Nice transferred the Gautier collection to the newly opened museum at the Palais Lascaris. Because of this transfer, the instrument now resides in a historical monument, enriching the cultural tapestry of Nice.

Paolo Antonio Testore, who crafted this petite basse de violon in Milan in 1717, followed in the footsteps of his father, Carlo Giuseppe Testore. Carlo Giuseppe had founded the Testore workshop and was known for his dedication to creating exquisite string instruments. Paolo Antonio's work, which continued this tradition, helped establish the Testore name as synonymous with quality and innovation in the world of string instruments. The instrument's classification as an early bass member of the violin family, larger than a modern cello, highlights its role in the evolution of symphonic music. Its presence at the Palais Lascaris underscores the museum's significance in preserving the history and artistry of musical craftsmanship.

Orientation: As you stand before the Harpe by Naderman, crafted in Paris in 1780, focus your gaze on the intricate carvings and gilded wood. This vantage reveals the refined elegance that made it a prized possession of the French aristocracy, a symbol of opulence at the cusp of revolutionary change.

In 1995, a remarkable discovery took place in the attic of the Château de Busset in the Allier department of France. There, the long-forgotten harp crafted by Jean-Henri Naderman in 1780 was found, having been out of sight for many years. This rediscovery led to the harp's eventual acquisition by the City of Nice in 2007, allowing it to be preserved and displayed in the Musée du Palais Lascaris. As a result, this exquisite instrument now stands as a testament to Naderman's craftsmanship, accessible to the public for appreciation and study.

The harp itself, a single-action pedal harp, employs the traditional crochet mechanism, allowing musicians to shorten strings by a semitone. This innovation was crucial in the late 18th century, permitting more complex harmonic explorations in compositions. The instrument's construction is a marvel of its time, made from carved, painted, and gilded wood. Its soundboard is adorned with symmetrical floral motifs, while a landscape scene framed by sculpted acanthus leaves graces its base. These decorative elements reflect the artistic tastes of the period, marrying function with aesthetic grandeur.

Interestingly, the harp once belonged to the Viscountess of Beaumont, an 18th-century French aristocrat. Its presence in her household signifies the cultural importance of such instruments among the elite, serving not only as a musical instrument but as a status symbol. The Palais Lascaris, now home to the second most important collection of musical instruments in France after the Musée de la Musique in Paris, provides a fitting backdrop for the harp. Situated in a historical monument, it offers a glimpse into the opulent world of the French court, just before the dawn of the Revolution. The harp’s delicate strings, once plucked in aristocratic salons, now echo through the halls of the museum, reminding us of a bygone era.

Orientation: Stand before the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, crafted in 1581 in Nuremberg. From this vantage point, observe the exquisite craftsmanship of the bell, which bears the maker's inscription, revealing its authenticity and age.

The Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer is an extraordinary relic from the cusp of the Renaissance, crafted in Nuremberg in 1581. It became part of Antoine Gautier's collection and was generously bequeathed to the city of Nice in 1901. This act transferred the instrument into the public collection of the Conservatoire National de Région de Nice. In 2001, the sackbut was permanently installed at the Palais Lascaris, a venue that celebrates its historical significance and craftsmanship.

This instrument is not only one of the earliest surviving sackbuts in original condition, but it also includes a contemporaneous brass mouthpiece, a rarity among 16th-century trombones. The bell rim of the instrument is inscribed with 'MACHT ANTONI SCHNITZER A[NNO] MDLXXXI', alongside Schnitzer's workshop device mark, which underscores the authenticity and provenance of this piece. The bore diameter at the entrance measures 10 mm, a detail that highlights the technical precision of the era.

The instrument's preservation in its original state offers a rare glimpse into the musical transitions from medieval to Renaissance periods. Unlike many of its contemporaries, which have undergone modifications over the centuries, this sackbut retains its original acoustics, providing insights into the soundscape of its time.

The Palais Lascaris, housed in a 17th-century aristocratic building, serves as an ideal location for this historical treasure. Its collection of over 500 instruments, one of the most significant in France, provides a context for understanding the evolution of musical instruments. The presence of the Schnitzer sackbut here not only connects us to the past but also invites reflection on the broader narrative of musical innovation.

As you recall the harp from earlier in your visit, consider how string and brass instruments evolved alongside one another, each influencing the course of music history in its unique way.

Orientation: Stand just to the right of the display case to catch the intricate carvings on the pegbox of William Turner's viola da gamba, a detail that embodies the unique craftsmanship of 17th-century London.

In 1652, William Turner crafted this six-string bass viola da gamba in London, demonstrating his prowess as a luthier. This particular viol, unlike many others that were transformed into cellos over time, retained its original form. It owes its preservation to Antoine Gautier, a Niçois musician and collector, who bequeathed it to the public collections of Nice in 1904. This instrument thus became part of the Palais Lascaris collection, where it is carefully maintained in playable condition. Remarkably, it is used for live concert performances in the palace's salons, offering a vivid link between the past and the present. 

Gautier's bequest significantly enhanced the museum's collection, integrating his passion with the palace’s mission to preserve musical history. The viol's continued use in concerts highlights its enduring musical value, contrasting with the sackbut you stopped at a moment ago, which remains a visual testament to its era. This particular piece serves not only as a historical artifact but also as a functional instrument, bridging centuries of musical tradition. As you contemplate this viol, consider what innovations in string instruments arose from Italy's renowned craftsmanship, a question that resonates deeply within this collection.

Orientation: Stand to the side of the Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore, where the light reveals the rich grain of its wood. From this angle, you'll notice the fine craftsmanship that links it to the violes gambe by William Turner, which you admired earlier.

In 1901, Antoine Gautier, a collector and amateur musician, bequeathed his collection of musical instruments, including the Testore basse de violon, to the city of Nice. This act of generosity was officially accepted by the city in September 1904. Then, in 1970, the City of Nice transferred the Gautier collection to the newly opened museum at the Palais Lascaris, securing a prestigious home for these historical treasures. Paolo Antonio Testore, who crafted this petite basse de violon in Milan in 1717, followed in the footsteps of his father, Carlo Giuseppe, who had established the Testore workshop in Milan, producing beautiful string instruments.

The petite basse de violon itself is larger than a modern cello and exemplifies the Italian mastery of string instrument craftsmanship during that era. This fine instrument, with its robust yet refined construction, is a testament to the Testore family's enduring legacy in lutherie. The Palais Lascaris, with its status as France's second most important collection of musical instruments, proudly displays Testore's work, highlighting the evolution of string instruments and their role in orchestral developments.

Orientation: Stand before the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) at the Palais Lascaris, and you'll be drawn into a world of 18th-century elegance. From here, you can appreciate the intricate floral motifs and gilded wood that showcase the harp's opulent craftsmanship.

In 1995, a significant discovery unfolded in the attic of the Château de Busset, located in the Allier department of France. A long-forgotten harp crafted by Jean-Henri Naderman in 1780 was unearthed, having been hidden away for many years. This rediscovery set in motion the harp's acquisition by the City of Nice in 2007, ensuring its preservation and display at the Musée du Palais Lascaris. François Joseph Naderman, Jean-Henri's son and a celebrated harpist and composer, further cemented the family's legacy by establishing the harp studio at the Paris Conservatory in 1825. This studio played a pivotal role in advancing the harp's development, fostering new techniques and compositions that enriched the instrument's repertoire.

This harp, a single-action pedal harp, employs the traditional crochet mechanism, allowing musicians to shorten strings by a semitone. The instrument's construction of carved, painted, and gilded wood, complete with a soundboard adorned with symmetrical floral motifs and a landscape scene framed by sculpted acanthus leaves, exemplifies the artistic grandeur of the era. Originally belonging to the Viscountess of Beaumont, the harp stands not only as a testament to Naderman's craftsmanship but also as a symbol of the cultural richness of pre-Revolutionary France. The Palais Lascaris, housing the second most important collection of musical instruments in France, offers a unique setting for this storied instrument. Its presence here, alongside over 500 other historical instruments, allows visitors to witness the evolution of musical craftsmanship and innovation.

Orientation: As you stand before the viola da gamba by William Turner from 1652, note its elegant lines and the rich patina of its wood, capturing the essence of 17th-century English craftsmanship. From this vantage point, appreciate the historic integrity of the instrument, untouched by the cello conversions that many of its counterparts underwent.

In 1652, William Turner crafted this six-string bass viola da gamba in London, a testament to his skill as a luthier. Unlike many of its contemporaries, which were later altered into cellos to fit changing musical tastes, this viol remained largely in its original form. Its preservation was a consequence of an important bequest by Antoine Gautier, a Niçois amateur musician, in 1904. This donation ensured that the viol became a part of the Palais Lascaris, where it is not just an exhibit but also maintained in playable condition. This allows it to be used for live concert performances, bridging the gap between the past and present.

Interestingly, Turner’s craftsmanship was celebrated during his lifetime, and his workshop in Gravel Lane near Aldgate was renowned for its innovative designs. Gautier's collection contained several historic instruments, and his donation included rare pieces like the Turner viol, enhancing Palais Lascaris's standing as a treasure trove of musical history. As you reflect on this piece, consider the Italian innovations in string instruments that were contemporaneous with Turner, setting the stage for the evolution of musical expression. This particular viol, with its unaltered design, continues to offer insights into the musical aesthetics of a bygone era, linking us to the 17th-century soundscape.

Orientation: Stand close to Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore (Milan, 1717) to observe the detailed craftsmanship, where the warm tones of the wooden body and the instrument's distinctive curves reveal its maker's mastery.

The journey of this bass viol began with Antoine Gautier, a passionate collector and amateur musician, who bequeathed his collection of musical instruments, including this petite basse de violon, to the city of Nice in 1901. Gautier's collection was officially accepted by the city in September 1904, marking the beginning of its journey through various prestigious locations until it reached its current residence. In 1970, the City of Nice transferred the Gautier collection to the then-newly opened Palais Lascaris, a historical monument now home to France's second most important collection of musical instruments.

The petite basse de violon was crafted in 1717 by Paolo Antonio Testore, who followed the family tradition established by his father, Carlo Giuseppe Testore. The instrument itself is larger than a modern cello, showcasing the evolution of the string family. The Testore family's legacy of fine craftsmanship is evident in the instrument's sound quality, a result of meticulous work passed down through generations. This piece not only reflects the individual skill of Paolo Antonio but also the broader Italian tradition of string instrument making, which set the stage for future symphonic developments, bridging the gap between baroque forms and contemporary orchestral sounds.

Orientation: Stand close to the glass case that houses the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, crafted in Nuremberg in 1581. From here, you can appreciate the intricacies of its design, including the maker's inscription on the bell rim that reads 'MACHT ANTONI SCHNITZER A[NNO] MDLXXXI', providing a direct link to its creator.

The Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, crafted in Nuremberg in 1581, became part of Antoine Gautier's collection when he bequeathed it to the city of Nice in 1901. This action transferred the instrument into the public collection of the Conservatoire National de Région de Nice. In 2001, the instrument underwent another significant change when it was permanently installed at the Palais Lascaris, a museum dedicated to historical musical instruments. This relocation allowed the instrument to be displayed in a venue that highlights its historical significance and craftsmanship.

Anton Schnitzer, the renowned brass instrument maker from Nuremberg, crafted this sackbut during a time when brass instruments were evolving in complexity and capability. His work was known for its precision and artistic detail, contributing significantly to the music of the Renaissance era. This particular instrument, with its original brass mouthpiece, is one of only four surviving 16th-century trombones to retain such a rare feature.

The sackbut's journey through history transformed it from a functional musical instrument into a cherished historical artifact. Gautier, a local amateur musician, recognized the importance of preserving such pieces for future generations. His decision to include the sackbut in his bequest has allowed visitors today to witness a tangible connection to the past. The instrument's placement at the Palais Lascaris underscores the museum's role in safeguarding musical heritage, showing how the evolution of brass instruments paralleled the broader transformations in musical practice during the Renaissance. The distinctive bore diameter of 10 mm not only highlights Schnitzer's craftsmanship but also illustrates the technical advancements that would pave the way for modern trombones. Now, as you reflect on the harp from earlier in your visit, consider how string and brass instruments have evolved side by side, shaping the auditory landscape of their time.

Orientation: Stand at the entrance of the music room at Palais Lascaris to view "Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780)." From here, you can appreciate the harp's intricate carvings and gilding that whisper tales of 18th-century aristocratic elegance.

In 1995, a harp crafted by Jean-Henri Naderman in 1780 was rediscovered in the attic of the Château de Busset in France. This fortuitous find led to its acquisition by the City of Nice in 2007, ensuring its preservation at the Musée du Palais Lascaris. Jean-Henri Naderman, a master luthier from Paris, constructed this harp with carved, painted, and gilded wood, employing a traditional crochet mechanism that shortens the strings by a semitone. This mechanism allowed musicians to produce nuanced melodies during a time of musical flourish in France. Before its years of obscurity, the harp belonged to the Viscountess of Beaumont, linking it to the elegant social circles of its time.

François Joseph Naderman, Jean-Henri's son, also contributed significantly to the harp's legacy. He established the harp studio at the Paris Conservatory in 1825, furthering the instrument's prestige and accessibility. This harp, now part of the Palais Lascaris collection, is surrounded by over 500 historical instruments, making the museum's collection the second most significant in France after the Musée de la Musique de la Philharmonie in Paris. The journey of Naderman's harp is not just about its rediscovery but also about the preservation of a family legacy, beautifully encapsulated in the strings that once echoed through French salons.

Orientation: Stand slightly to the left of Violes gambe by William Turner to appreciate the intricate carved head and pegbox, perfectly preserved since its creation.

In 1652, William Turner crafted this six-string bass viola da gamba in his London workshop. An exceptional instrument, it survived the common fate of many 17th-century viols, which were often modified into cellos to suit evolving tastes. Its pristine condition is owed to Antoine Gautier, a Niçois amateur musician and dedicated collector, who bequeathed the viol to the public collections of Nice in 1904. The instrument then became part of the Palais Lascaris collection. Here, it is not merely a static exhibit; it is maintained in playable condition and features in live concert performances at the palace. This viol is part of a collection of over 500 historical instruments, demonstrating a rich history of musical craftsmanship. Turner's viol stands alongside other great pieces, like the tenor sackbut you saw earlier, showcasing the deep resonant tones that captivated England’s composers and listeners in the 17th century.

Orientation: Stand directly before the Basse de violon by Paolo Antonio Testore, Milano, 1717. Notice the instrument’s elegant proportions and robust form, hinting at the rich sound it would have produced, larger than that of the violes gambe by Turner you saw earlier.

In 1901, Antoine Gautier, a dedicated collector and enthusiastic musician, bequeathed his invaluable collection of musical instruments, including this Testore basse de violon, to the city of Nice. By September 1904, the city officially accepted Gautier's bequest, marking the beginning of its long journey through various local institutions. Finally, in 1970, the collection found a permanent home at the Palais Lascaris, securing its place within one of France's most prestigious musical instrument collections. Paolo Antonio Testore, who crafted this petite basse de violon in Milan in 1717, followed in the prestigious footsteps of his father Carlo Giuseppe Testore, producing instruments that exemplified Italian string mastery. The Testore family's commitment to quality is evident in the instrument's design, renowned for its durability and rich tonal quality, which were essential features in earlier orchestral developments. This bass viol's presence at Palais Lascaris underscores the institution's commitment to preserving musical heritage, aligning with the collection’s rediscovery and ultimate restoration to public admiration.

Orientation: As you stand beside the six-string bass viola da gamba by William Turner, you'll notice its delicately preserved original carved head and pegbox, offering a rare glimpse into the craftsmanship of 1652 London. Move closer, and you'll catch the details that survived centuries nearly untouched.

In 1652, William Turner created this viola da gamba in London, showcasing his skill as a luthier in an era when England was bustling with musical innovation. Unlike many viols that faced transformation over time, this instrument remained true to its original form. This significant preservation was made possible by Antoine Gautier, a Niçois amateur musician, who bequeathed it to the public collections in Nice in 1904. Gautier's donation ensured the viol's continuity in its original state, eventually placing it in the Palais Lascaris. Here, it not only complements the museum’s impressive collection of over 500 instruments but also remains in playable condition. The viol's enduring capacity for performance allows audiences to experience an authentic piece of the 17th-century soundscape, bridging the centuries in a tangible, auditory manner. How did the Italian focus on craftsmanship contribute to the evolution of string instruments beyond this era?

Orientation: Stand before the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) at the Palais Lascaris in Nice and let your eyes wander over the intricate carvings and gilded embellishments. From this vantage point, you'll appreciate the delicately painted floral motifs and the acoustic engineering that made this instrument a marvel of its time.

In 1780, Jean-Henri Naderman, a renowned luthier based in Paris, crafted the harp before you. He used carved, painted, and gilded wood, employing a traditional single-action pedal and crochet mechanism, which allowed musicians to alter string length by a semitone. This innovation enabled more complex compositions and nuanced performances, cementing his reputation in the realm of French musical instruments. The harp was initially owned by the Viscountess of Beaumont, integrating it into the elegant social circles of 18th-century France.

In 1995, the harp was rediscovered in the attic of the Château de Busset in France, long after it had fallen into obscurity. Its revival led to the City of Nice acquiring it in 2007, ensuring its preservation and subsequent display at the Musée du Palais Lascaris. This acquisition placed the harp among the second most significant collection of musical instruments in France, right after the Musée de la Musique de la Philharmonie in Paris.

Jean-Henri Naderman's legacy continued through his son, François Joseph Naderman, who established the harp studio at the Paris Conservatory in 1825. François fought to preserve his father's designs while advancing harp craftsmanship, influencing the next generation of musicians. Now housed among over 500 instruments, the Harpe by Naderman (Paris, 1780) stands as an emblem of both artistic beauty and technological advancement at a time when the French court reveled in opulence. Its history invites us to ponder what sounds filled its strings and echoed through the halls of aristocratic gatherings long ago.

Orientation: Stand before the 1581 Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, here at the Palais Lascaris. Look closely at this exquisite brass creation to appreciate the craftsmanship and historical resonance it carries. From this position, you can see the maker's mark inscribed on the bell rim, a trace of its origins in Nuremberg.

The Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer, crafted in Nuremberg in 1581, is a testament to the artistry of its maker, Anton Schnitzer the Elder. Schnitzer specialized in creating ceremonial brass instruments for the Bavarian court, and this sackbut embodies the precision and artistic flair for which he was renowned. It was part of Antoine Gautier's collection when he bequeathed it to the city of Nice in 1901. This act transferred the instrument into the public collection of the Conservatoire National de Région de Nice, preserving its historical integrity.

In 2001, the instrument underwent another significant transition when it was permanently installed at the Palais Lascaris. This relocation offered it a place within the museum's collection, highlighting its historical significance as one of the earliest surviving sackbuts in original condition and featuring a contemporaneous brass mouthpiece. The ten-millimeter bore of the instrument is evidence of the period's technical expertise in acoustics, bridging medieval music traditions with the Renaissance's evolving soundscapes.

With the original inscription 'MACHT ANTONI SCHNITZER A[NNO] MDLXXXI' visible on its bell, the sackbut tells the story of its own creation and journey through time. How did such brass giants evolve alongside string instruments, like the harp by Naderman you admired earlier? The Palais Lascaris, as France’s second most important collection of musical instruments, invites further exploration of these musical evolutions.

Orientation: Stand close to the Sacqueboute ténor by Anton Schnitzer to admire the intricate craftsmanship on its brass body. From this vantage point, you’ll notice the finely engraved inscription on the bell rim, denoting its creation in Nuremberg in 1581.

The Sacqueboute ténor, crafted by Anton Schnitzer in 1581, is a remarkable relic from the Renaissance period. Schnitzer, an esteemed brass instrument maker active in Nuremberg during the 16th century, was known for the precision and artistry of his work. His creations were highly sought after, particularly by musicians of the Bavarian court. This specific sackbut entered the realm of public ownership when Antoine Gautier, a local musician and collector, bequeathed it to the city of Nice in 1901. This act enriched the Conservatoire National de Région de Nice’s collection, providing a tangible link to the musical past. In 2001, the instrument underwent another transformation as it became a permanent exhibit at the Palais Lascaris, a museum that specializes in historical musical instruments.

Notably, the sackbut still retains its original brass mouthpiece, a rarity among 16th-century instruments, indicating its excellent preservation over centuries. The inscription on the bell bears Schnitzer's name and the date of creation, marking it as an artifact of both artistic and historical significance. Situated within the grand Palais Lascaris, this instrument provides insight into the evolution of brass instruments from their medieval roots to the modern trombone. As you take in the craftsmanship of one of the oldest surviving sackbuts, recall the harp from Paris that you encountered earlier on this tour. Together, these instruments showcase how both string and brass families evolved, each influencing musical traditions across centuries. As you move through the rest of the collection, consider how innovations in both brass and strings created the rich tapestry of sound we appreciate today.

Reflecting on the harp from earlier in your visit, consider how string instruments evolved alongside these brass giants, shaping the contours of musical history.
